lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: mini-runtime
text: Hi everyone, and welcome to JavaScript Deep Dive. In this course we are not going to learn new syntax. You already know how to write functions, loops and callbacks. What we are going to do is go underneath all of that and understand what the engine is actually doing when your code runs. And the way we will do it is by building something. Over the next lectures we will build a small project called mini-runtime, a tiny model of the JavaScript runtime, written in JavaScript itself. I know that sounds a little circular, but you'll see it works really well, because a model you wrote yourself is a model you can never forget.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: mini-runtime
text: So let me tell you what mini-runtime will contain. There will be four pieces. First, a call stack, in a file called callstack.js, where we push and pop execution contexts. Second, a scope-chain resolver in scope.js, which answers the question, when I write the name x, which x do I mean? Third, a prototype lookup in proto.js, which walks the prototype chain the way the engine does. And fourth, an event-loop simulator in eventloop.js, which decides what runs next when the stack is empty. Then a small file called runtime.js will wire all four together so we can run little programs through it.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: mini-runtime
text: Now why build it this way? Because most JavaScript confusion comes from a wrong mental model, not from missing facts. People say hoisting moves your code to the top of the file. It doesn't. People say classes are a new kind of object system. They aren't. People say setTimeout with zero runs immediately. It doesn't. Each of those is a model problem. When we build the machine ourselves, step by step, each of those sentences will fall apart on its own, and you will replace them with something that is actually true and that you can predict with.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: mini-runtime
text: Here is how the course is laid out. Chapter one is about execution, how source text becomes running code and what a call stack really is. Chapter two covers scope, hoisting and closures. Chapter three is about this and the new keyword. Chapter four is prototypes and classes, including writing Object.create and instanceof by hand. Chapter five goes into the V8 engine, hidden classes and inline caches. Chapter six is the event loop, microtasks and async await. And in chapter seven we take one nasty bug and trace it through every layer we built, so you see the whole thing working together.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: mini-runtime
text: Before we move on, a word about how to get the most out of this. Every lecture ends with working code in the mini-runtime folder, and every lecture begins by running what we wrote last time. If something from a previous lecture is fuzzy, don't push forward, go back, because the pieces stack. I'd also suggest keeping a scratch file called notes.js, where you try small experiments that come to mind. Real understanding comes from poking the machine and being surprised by it, and that is the habit I most want you to leave this course with.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: mini-runtime
text: A couple of ground rules before we start. I'll be using plain Node.js, a recent version, so you only need a terminal and an editor. Please type along with me instead of copying, because the typing is where the learning happens. Create an empty folder called mini-runtime, run npm init with the dash y flag, and make a file called callstack.js, even if it's empty for now. When something surprises you, stop the video and run the experiment yourself. Okay? In the next lecture we will follow a single line of source code all the way from text to execution. Let's go.

lecture_title: 1.2 - From Source Text to Running Code
text: In the last lecture we planned mini-runtime. Today I want to answer a very basic question that most people never ask. When you run node index.js, what actually happens between the text in that file and the output on your screen? Because until you can describe that journey, words like compile, interpret and parse are just noise. So let's walk through it. The journey has a few stages, and we'll go through each one briefly, then we will build a tiny version of the first stages in our project so they stop being abstract.

lecture_title: 1.2 - From Source Text to Running Code
text: Stage one is parsing. The engine receives a string of characters. It first runs a tokenizer, sometimes called a lexer, that chops the string into tokens. So the text `let total = 1 + 2;` becomes the keyword let, an identifier total, an equals sign, a number, a plus, another number and a semicolon. Then the parser takes those tokens and builds a tree, the abstract syntax tree, or AST. That tree says, this is a variable declaration, its name is total, its initial value is a binary expression with a plus operator. Notice that the tree has already thrown away whitespace and comments. It's pure structure.

lecture_title: 1.2 - From Source Text to Running Code
text: Here's a detail that matters later. V8 doesn't fully parse every function up front. It does a quick pre-parse of functions that haven't been called yet, just enough to find syntax errors and figure out variable scopes, and it does the full parse lazily when the function is first called. That's why a syntax error anywhere in your file stops the whole script before a single line runs, but a huge unused function doesn't cost you much startup time. Parsing also records which variables each function uses from outside itself, and that information is exactly what we'll need when we build scope resolution in chapter two.

lecture_title: 1.2 - From Source Text to Running Code
text: Stage two is turning the tree into something executable. In V8 the AST goes to an interpreter called Ignition, which produces bytecode, a compact list of simple instructions, and starts running it immediately. While it runs, V8 watches which functions are hot, meaning called a lot. Those get handed to an optimizing compiler, TurboFan, which generates machine code based on assumptions about the types it has seen. If an assumption breaks, the engine throws the optimized code away and falls back to bytecode. We'll return to this in chapter five when we talk about hidden classes. For now, just hold the picture, parse, bytecode, optimize when hot.

lecture_title: 1.2 - From Source Text to Running Code
text: A quick recap so the picture sticks. Text goes to tokens, tokens go to a tree, the tree goes to bytecode, and hot bytecode goes to optimized machine code that can be thrown away if its assumptions fail. Two things from this will come back again and again. One, the parser already knows the scope structure before anything runs. Two, the optimizer makes bets based on the shapes and types it sees. Keep both in your head, because chapters two and five are built on them.

lecture_title: 1.2 - From Source Text to Running Code
text: Let's make this concrete in the project. Open a new file called parse-demo.js, and just to look at a real tree, I'll paste a small tokenizer that splits on spaces and symbols and prints an array. I'm not asking you to build a full parser, that would be a whole course by itself. The point is to see that your code is data before it is behavior. Once you see that, the next question is natural. When this data starts executing, where does the engine keep track of what's currently running? That's the call stack and execution contexts, and that's our next lecture.

lecture_title: 1.3 - Execution Contexts and the Call Stack
text: Let's start building. In the previous lecture we saw that source text becomes a tree and then bytecode. Now we ask, while bytecode is running, how does the engine keep track of where it is? The answer is the call stack, and the things on the stack are called execution contexts. Today we create callstack.js in mini-runtime, and by the end you'll have a working stack that you can push to, pop from, and print as a stack trace, the same kind of trace you see when an error is thrown.

lecture_title: 1.3 - Execution Contexts and the Call Stack
text: First the idea. An execution context is a record the engine creates every time code starts running. There's a global one when your script starts, and a new one every time you call a function. Each context holds the information that code needs, which variables are in scope, what the value of this is, and where to continue when the function returns. Because function calls nest, the contexts nest, and the natural structure for that is a stack, last in, first out. The function you called most recently must finish first, so it sits on top.

lecture_title: 1.3 - Execution Contexts and the Call Stack
text: Now the code. In callstack.js I'll write a class called CallStack with an array called frames. Then a method push that takes a name and an environment, creates an object `{ name, env, startedAt }`, and pushes it onto frames. Then pop, which removes and returns the last frame, and throws an error if the stack is empty, because popping an empty stack is always a bug in our runtime. And a method called peek that returns the top frame without removing it. I also want a depth getter that returns frames dot length, we'll use it for recursion limits in a moment.

lecture_title: 1.3 - Execution Contexts and the Call Stack
text: Let's add a stack trace. A method called trace that maps over frames from top to bottom and joins the names with a newline and the text at, so it prints the same shape as a real stack trace in Node. Try it. Push main, push outer, push inner, then call trace, and you see inner, outer, main from top to bottom. Now the famous error. Add a constant MAX_DEPTH of, say, ten thousand, and in push, if depth is at or above it, throw a RangeError with the message Maximum call stack size exceeded. That is literally what recursion without a base case runs into.

lecture_title: 1.3 - Execution Contexts and the Call Stack
text: Let me finish with a check for understanding. Suppose function a calls b, and b calls c, and c throws an error. What does the stack look like at the moment of the throw, and what happens to the frames afterward? The answer is c, b, a, global from top to bottom, and the error unwinds the stack, popping each frame until something catches it. If nothing does, the program ends with that trace. We'll reuse this unwinding idea when we model errors later, so make sure it feels natural.

lecture_title: 1.3 - Execution Contexts and the Call Stack
text: Let me connect this to the real engine, because I want you to leave with the right picture. Node's stack limit is not a number of frames, it's a size in memory, roughly a megabyte by default, so the real depth depends on how big each frame is. You can see this yourself by writing a recursive function that increments a counter and catches the RangeError, then printing the counter. Run it with a function that has many local variables and again with an empty one and the numbers differ. Okay, so we have a stack. But what goes inside each frame's env? That's scope, and that's chapter two, starting with the scope chain.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Lexical Scope and the Scope Chain
text: Welcome to chapter two. We have a call stack, and each frame has an env field that we've left as an empty object. Today we fill it in. The question is, when your code says the name total, how does the engine know which total you mean? The answer is lexical scope, and the data structure behind it is the scope chain. We'll write scope.js with a Scope class, and by the end you'll have a resolver that follows the same rules as the real language.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Lexical Scope and the Scope Chain
text: The word lexical is the key. It means scope is decided by where the code is written, not by where it's called from. If I write a function inside another function, the inner function can see the outer function's variables, because of the physical position of the text. You can read a program and draw its scopes with a pencil, without running anything. The opposite idea, dynamic scope, where the caller's variables are visible, exists in some old languages and shell scripts, but JavaScript doesn't work that way, and the confusion between the two causes a lot of bugs.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Lexical Scope and the Scope Chain
text: Now let's model it. In scope.js I'll create a class Scope with a constructor that takes a parent, which can be null, and creates a Map called bindings. Then a method declare, taking a name and a value, that sets it in bindings. And the important one, lookup, which takes a name. If this scope's bindings has the name, return the value. Otherwise, if there is a parent, return parent dot lookup of the name. And if there is no parent, throw a ReferenceError saying the name is not defined. That recursion up the parent links is the scope chain.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Lexical Scope and the Scope Chain
text: Let's test with a tiny program in our model. Create a global scope with no parent and declare a as one. Create a child scope whose parent is global and declare b as two. Look up a from the child and you get one, because the lookup walks up. Look up b from global and you get a ReferenceError, because scope links only point outward, never inward. Now declare a as ten in the child, and look it up. You get ten, and the global a is still one. That's shadowing, the inner binding hides the outer one without changing it.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Lexical Scope and the Scope Chain
text: Let me give you a practical use of this right now. When you're debugging and a variable has an unexpected value, ask which scope the engine finds it in, by walking outward from the use site one scope at a time. Nine times out of ten the answer is that you shadowed something by accident, a parameter with the same name as an outer variable, or a block variable hiding a function variable. Node's debugger and the browser devtools both show the scope chain explicitly, so go and look at it once, okay?

lecture_title: 2.1 - Lexical Scope and the Scope Chain
text: One more thing about the real language. Where does a new scope get created? Function bodies create one, and so do blocks, but only for let, const and class declarations. A var ignores block boundaries and attaches to the nearest function. We'll add that distinction to our Scope class with a kind field, either function or block. It's a small change, but it explains the classic loop bug with var. And it leads straight to our next topic, because if declarations are registered before code runs, then what does it mean to use a variable before its line? That's hoisting.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone
text: Last time we built Scope with declare and lookup. Today's topic is one of the most misunderstood words in JavaScript, hoisting. Most explanations say the engine moves your declarations to the top of the file. I want to replace that with the true version, because the true version is simpler and it predicts the behavior of let and const correctly, which the move to the top story can't do. So today we correct the story, and we'll model it properly in scope.js.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone
text: Here is the truth. Before a scope's code runs, the engine does a pass through the scope and creates bindings for every declaration in it. Nothing moves in the source. The bindings just exist from the start of the scope, and what differs is how they are initialized. A var declaration is created and immediately initialized to undefined. A function declaration is created and initialized to the whole function. A let or const declaration is created but left uninitialized. Three different starting states, and that's all hoisting is.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone
text: Let's see what that means. Write console.log of a, then var a equals five. It prints undefined, because the binding existed and was undefined. Now write console.log of b, then let b equals five. You get a ReferenceError, cannot access b before initialization. The binding exists, the engine knows about it, which is why it doesn't say b is not defined, but it's in a state called the temporal dead zone, from the start of the scope until the line with the declaration runs. Temporal, because it's about time, not about position in the text.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone
text: Now let's put this into mini-runtime. In scope.js I'll add a method called hoist that takes a list of declarations, each with a name and a kind. For var, it calls declare with undefined. For function, it declares with the function value. For let and const, it stores a special symbol called UNINITIALIZED. Then in lookup, if the value we find is that symbol, we throw a ReferenceError saying cannot access the name before initialization. And we add an initialize method that replaces the symbol when the declaration line executes. Run the example from before and our model behaves exactly like Node.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone
text: So what should you do in practice with all this? Prefer const by default, and let when you need to reassign, and avoid var. That way you never depend on the undefined initial state, and any early use fails loudly with a clear ReferenceError rather than silently giving you undefined. And declare things before using them, even for functions, even though function declarations would work. The model is clear now, so the code you write should not rely on its odd corners.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone
text: Two gotchas to finish. First, function expressions are not hoisted like declarations. If you write var greet equals a function, then greet is undefined until that line, and calling it early throws a TypeError, greet is not a function. Second, the typeof operator used to be safe on undeclared names, but it throws inside the temporal dead zone. That surprised a lot of people when let arrived. Both of these follow from the model. Next lecture, we'll look at what happens when a function leaves its scope and still needs it. That's closures.

lecture_title: 2.3 - Closures: Functions That Remember Their Scope
text: This is the lecture where scope pays off. A closure is a function together with the scope it was created in. That's the entire definition. People make it sound mystical, but with the Scope class we built it is almost trivial, and today we'll see why. We'll make functions in mini-runtime carry a reference to their defining scope, and then we'll watch a counter survive after the function that made it has returned. Let's go through it slowly, since everything we did so far leads here.

lecture_title: 2.3 - Closures: Functions That Remember Their Scope
text: Start with the classic example in real JavaScript. A function makeCounter declares let count equals zero and returns a function that increments count and returns it. Call makeCounter, store the result as next, and call next three times. You get one, two, three. Here's the puzzle. makeCounter has returned. Its execution context was popped off the call stack. So where is count living? If variables lived on the stack, it would be gone. It isn't gone, because the scope object isn't stored on the stack. It's an ordinary object on the heap, and the returned function holds a reference to it.

lecture_title: 2.3 - Closures: Functions That Remember Their Scope
text: So in our model we add one thing. When a function is created, we record the current scope on it. In runtime.js I'll write createFunction, taking a name, params, a body, and the current scope, and returning an object `{ name, params, body, closure: scope }`. Then in callFunction, instead of making a new scope whose parent is the caller's scope, we make one whose parent is fn dot closure. That single line is the difference between lexical and dynamic scope, and it's the entire closure mechanism.

lecture_title: 2.3 - Closures: Functions That Remember Their Scope
text: Let's run it. Build makeCounter in our model, call it, keep the returned function, call it three times, and print. We get one, two, three. Then create a second counter and notice it starts from one again, because each call to makeCounter created a fresh Scope with its own count. Two closures, two scope objects, no sharing. This is also why closures are used for private state. Nobody outside can reach count, because the only access is through the function that holds the scope.

lecture_title: 2.3 - Closures: Functions That Remember Their Scope
text: To close, let's recap what we built. Functions now carry a closure field, calls create a scope whose parent is that field, and scopes live on the heap so they outlive stack frames. Our callstack.js still pushes and pops frames, but the frame's env is now a Scope whose chain can reach back to where the function was defined. Notice how little code that took. Closures aren't a feature that was added to the language, they're what you get automatically from lexical scope plus first-class functions.

lecture_title: 2.3 - Closures: Functions That Remember Their Scope
text: Now the famous loop bug. A for loop with var i, pushing functions into an array that log i, then calling them after the loop prints the final value every time, because all the functions share the one function-level scope and its single i. Change var to let, and each iteration gets its own block scope, so each function sees its own i. In our model that's just creating a new Scope per iteration. One last warning, closures keep the whole scope alive, which can hold large objects in memory, so release references you don't need. Next chapter we deal with this, the value of this.

lecture_title: 3.1 - How this Gets Bound: The Four Rules
text: Now we get to the most argued-about keyword in JavaScript, this. And the good news is that it follows exactly four rules, and once you know them you can predict this by reading the call site. Not the function definition, the call site, which is the single most important thing to take from today. So we'll learn the four rules, then add them to mini-runtime so callFunction can compute a value of this for every call.

lecture_title: 3.1 - How this Gets Bound: The Four Rules
text: Rule one, default binding. If you call a plain function, like greet with parentheses and nothing in front, then this is the global object, or undefined in strict mode. Modules and classes are always strict, so in most modern code you get undefined. That's why pulling a method off an object and calling it alone loses its this. Rule two, implicit binding. If you call it as obj dot method, then this is the object in front of the dot. Only the last object counts, so a dot b dot method gives this equal to b.

lecture_title: 3.1 - How this Gets Bound: The Four Rules
text: Rule three, explicit binding. Using call, apply or bind lets you choose this directly. Call and apply invoke the function immediately, with arguments listed or in an array. Bind returns a new function with this permanently fixed. Rule four, new binding. If you call a function with the new keyword, a fresh object is created and this points to it. We'll implement that one in the next lecture. The priority order, if rules conflict, is new first, then explicit, then implicit, then default. Bind beats a dot call, for example.

lecture_title: 3.1 - How this Gets Bound: The Four Rules
text: Arrow functions are the exception, and they're not a fifth rule. An arrow function has no this of its own. It looks up this the same way it looks up any variable, through the scope chain, so it takes the this of the scope where it was written. That's lexical, like everything else we built. It also means call, apply and bind can't change an arrow's this. This is why arrows are great for callbacks inside methods, and a bad idea for object methods that need their own object.

lecture_title: 3.1 - How this Gets Bound: The Four Rules
text: A quick exercise before we leave this. Take an object with a name property and a method that logs this dot name. Call it directly and it works. Assign the method to a variable and call that, and you get undefined or an error. Pass it to setTimeout, same problem. Now fix it three ways, with bind, with an arrow wrapper, and with a class field arrow function. For each fix, say which rule is now in play. If you can do that, you've got this.

lecture_title: 3.1 - How this Gets Bound: The Four Rules
text: Let's code it. In runtime.js, callFunction now takes a thisArg parameter. I'll write a helper resolveThis that takes the call description. If the call has isNew, create an object. If it has an explicit receiver from call or bind, use that. If it has an object before the dot, use it. Otherwise return undefined, because our runtime is strict. Store the result in the new scope under the name this. For arrows, skip storing it, so lookup walks outward. Test with a detached method, and you'll see undefined. Next, constructors and what new really does.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Constructor Functions and the new Keyword
text: In the last lecture we listed four binding rules and left the last one, new, for today. The new keyword looks like magic, but it's a short recipe, four steps, and once you can write those steps in code you will never be confused by constructors again. We'll implement a function called construct in runtime.js, and along the way we'll meet the first real piece of prototype machinery, which prepares us for chapter four. So let's build it.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Constructor Functions and the new Keyword
text: Here is the setup in plain JavaScript. A constructor function is just a normal function that we call with new, by convention with a capital letter. function Dog taking a name, setting this dot name equals name. Then new Dog, with the string Rex, gives us an object with a name property. Nothing in the function created that object. We never wrote return. So who did? The new operator did, and the steps are the same every time. Take a moment to see that this is a pattern you've used many times.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Constructor Functions and the new Keyword
text: The four steps. One, create a brand new empty object. Two, set that object's internal prototype to the constructor's prototype property, which is where the object will look for things it doesn't have. Three, call the constructor with this bound to the new object, passing along the arguments. Four, if the constructor returned an object, use that as the result, otherwise use the new object from step one. Step four is a rarely used detail, but it's why returning a primitive from a constructor is simply ignored.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Constructor Functions and the new Keyword
text: Now in code. In runtime.js I'll write construct, taking a function and an args array. First, `const obj = Object.create(fn.prototype)`, which does steps one and two in one go. Next we call the function through callFunction with the thisArg set to obj. Store that in result. Then `return (typeof result === 'object' && result !== null) || typeof result === 'function' ? result : obj`. That's all of new. Try it with Dog, and check that Object.getPrototypeOf of the result is Dog dot prototype. It is.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Constructor Functions and the new Keyword
text: A common mistake is forgetting new. If you call Dog without it, the default binding rule applies, so this is undefined in strict code and the assignment throws, or it quietly sets a property on the global object in sloppy mode. That's why ES6 classes throw an error if called without new, and why older code had a check at the top, if this is not an instance of Dog, return new Dog. Both are guarding against the same thing. You now understand why that guard existed.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Constructor Functions and the new Keyword
text: And this tells us where methods should go. If I write this dot bark equals a function inside Dog, every instance gets its own copy of that function, and a thousand dogs means a thousand functions. If I instead write Dog dot prototype dot bark, there is one function, and every dog finds it through the link set in step two. That link, and how lookup follows it, is the topic of the whole next chapter. Take a break, then we go into prototype inheritance, and we'll write proto.js.

lecture_title: 4.1 - Prototype Inheritance
text: Welcome to chapter four. We finished the last chapter with new setting up a link between an object and its constructor's prototype. Today we find out what that link is for, and we write proto.js, the prototype lookup of mini-runtime. This is the topic that trips up more developers than any other in the language, so I'll go slowly. And I'll start with a definition that I want you to hear carefully, because everything else this chapter hangs off it.

lecture_title: 4.1 - Prototype Inheritance
text: Prototype inheritance is the mechanism by which objects in JavaScript inherit properties and methods from other objects. Every JavaScript object has an internal link to another object called its prototype, accessible as __proto__. When you access a property on an object and JavaScript cannot find it directly on that object, it walks up the prototype chain automatically until it either finds the property or reaches null at the top of the chain. This prototype lookup is invisible to you but happens on every single property access.

lecture_title: 4.1 - Prototype Inheritance
text: Let's see this live. Open a Node REPL and type `const animal = { eats: true }`, then `const dog = Object.create(animal)`. Now `dog.eats` gives true, even though dog has no own property called eats. Check with `dog.hasOwnProperty('eats')`, which is false. And `Object.getPrototypeOf(dog) === animal` is true. Next set `dog.barks = true`. That goes on dog itself, not on animal, because assignment always writes to the object you are assigning on. Reading walks the chain, writing doesn't. Keep that asymmetry in mind, it explains a lot of surprising bugs.

lecture_title: 4.1 - Prototype Inheritance
text: Think of prototype inheritance as a delegation chain, not a copy. If object A has object B as its prototype, and you look for a method on A that does not exist there, JavaScript automatically delegates the lookup to B. This chain continues all the way up to Object.prototype which is the root. The key insight is that objects do not copy properties from their prototype. They delegate lookups to it at runtime. This delegation model is what makes prototype inheritance both powerful and memory-efficient. All instances share one copy of inherited methods rather than each having their own copy.

lecture_title: 4.1 - Prototype Inheritance
text: Now let's model it in proto.js. I'll write a function getProperty taking an object and a key. Inside, a loop with `let current = obj`, and while current is not null, if current has its own key, return its value, otherwise set current to Object.getPrototypeOf of current. After the loop, return undefined. That's the whole lookup, about six lines. Let me also write setProperty, which just does `obj[key] = value`, because writes ignore the chain, with one exception, setters, which we'll skip. Test it with the animal and dog we made, and a three-level chain, and watch it climb.

lecture_title: 4.1 - Prototype Inheritance
text: Let me show where all those built-in methods come from. Create an empty object and call `toString` on it. You never defined that. It's found on Object.prototype, which sits at the top, and its own prototype is null. An array goes one level deeper, the array's prototype is Array.prototype, which holds map and filter, and whose prototype is Object.prototype. That's why arrays also have hasOwnProperty. And since the chain is live, if you add a method to a prototype, every existing object sees it immediately. Powerful, and also why modifying built-in prototypes is considered dangerous.

lecture_title: 4.1 - Prototype Inheritance
text: When you use the class syntax in modern JavaScript it is still prototype-based inheritance under the hood. The class keyword is purely syntactic sugar. When you write class Dog extends Animal, JavaScript sets up the prototype chain so that Dog.prototype has Animal.prototype as its prototype. The instanceof operator also relies on this chain to check if an object was derived from a particular constructor function. Understanding the prototype chain helps you debug unexpected behavior when properties seem to appear from nowhere or when you accidentally shadow a prototype method.

lecture_title: 4.1 - Prototype Inheritance
text: One more debugging tip before we move on. When a property shows up from nowhere, use a loop that walks the chain and prints each object that has that key as an own property. We can build that straight from getProperty, we'll call it findOwner, returning the object where the property was found. And when you see shadowing, where an own property hides one further up, findOwner will show you. Next time we dig into classes, and see that they are exactly what we've just built with nicer syntax.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Classes Are Sugar Over the Prototype Chain
text: Last lecture we built a prototype lookup. Now let's look at the thing most of you actually write, the class keyword. The claim today is that a class adds no new object model. It is a cleaner way of writing the constructor function and prototype dance we've already done. To prove it, we'll take a class and desugar it by hand, and then add class support to mini-runtime's proto.js in about twenty lines. Let's go step by step and see for ourselves.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Classes Are Sugar Over the Prototype Chain
text: Start with a class. `class Animal` with a constructor taking name and setting this dot name, and a method speak that logs the name. Check what you get. `typeof Animal` is function. `Animal.prototype.speak` is the method you wrote. `Animal.prototype.constructor === Animal` is true. So the class is a function, and the methods live on its prototype object, exactly like in the constructor-function version. A few differences exist, class bodies are strict, the methods aren't enumerable, and calling a class without new throws. But the structure is identical.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Classes Are Sugar Over the Prototype Chain
text: Now inheritance. `class Dog extends Animal`, with a constructor that calls super of name, then sets this dot tricks. What does extends actually do? Two links. One, `Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog.prototype)` equals Animal.prototype, so instances of Dog find speak through the chain. Two, `Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog)` equals Animal, so static methods are inherited too, which people often forget. A call to super is basically calling the parent constructor so that it initializes this. In a derived class you can't touch this before super returns, since the object is created by the base class.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Classes Are Sugar Over the Prototype Chain
text: Let's write the desugared version by hand in proto.js. A function defineClass takes a name, an optional parent, a constructor function and a methods object. It creates the function, then sets `fn.prototype = Object.create(parent ? parent.prototype : Object.prototype)`. Then it sets `fn.prototype.constructor = fn`, and copies each method onto fn.prototype. If there is a parent, it calls `Object.setPrototypeOf(fn, parent)` for statics. Return fn. Now define Animal and Dog with it, create a dog, call speak, and you'll see it works just like the real syntax.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Classes Are Sugar Over the Prototype Chain
text: Let me add a caution about how people use classes in JavaScript, because the sugar can hide costs. Inheritance hierarchies more than two levels deep make the chain longer, and every miss walks further. They also couple code tightly, a change in a base class ripples into everything below it. Many teams prefer composition, small objects combined together, or functions that return objects. Both styles are fine, but now that you know classes are just prototypes, you can choose with open eyes, instead of copying an object-oriented habit from another language, okay?

lecture_title: 4.2 - Classes Are Sugar Over the Prototype Chain
text: Here's a payoff for the model. Private fields with the hash prefix are different, they are not on the chain, they're stored in a hidden per-object slot, so they cannot be accessed by lookup at all. That's by design. Also, methods defined as arrow function class fields are own properties on each instance, not shared, so they cost memory per object, though they bind this lexically. Both of these become obvious once you ask, is it on the prototype or on the instance? In the next lecture we write the two operators that depend on this chain.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Writing Object.create and instanceof by Hand
text: Today's lecture is pure building. We've talked about the prototype chain for two lectures, and the best test of whether you really understand a mechanism is to write it yourself. So we will implement Object.create and instanceof from scratch in proto.js, without using the built-in versions. Along the way we'll use only two primitives that the language gives us, getPrototypeOf and setPrototypeOf, plus a function's prototype property. These are two of the most asked-about topics in interviews, and after today you will be able to answer with code, not just words.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Writing Object.create and instanceof by Hand
text: Let's begin with create. Object.create takes a prototype and returns a new empty object whose prototype is that value. Our version, myCreate, takes proto. First a guard, if proto is not an object and not null, throw a TypeError. Then there are two ways to build it. The modern way is `const obj = {}; Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, proto); return obj;`. The old way, which was the polyfill for years, creates a throwaway constructor `function F() {}`, sets `F.prototype = proto`, and returns `new F()`. Both give the same result, and the second one shows that new is doing the link for us.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Writing Object.create and instanceof by Hand
text: Test it. `const a = { x: 1 }; const b = myCreate(a);` Then `b.x` is one, and `Object.getPrototypeOf(b) === a` is true. Also try myCreate with null, and you get an object with no prototype at all, so `b.toString` is undefined. People use that to build pure dictionaries, where keys like constructor or hasOwnProperty can't collide with inherited names. One caveat is that setPrototypeOf on an existing object can slow V8 down, because it changes the object's shape after the fact. Remember that, we'll see why in chapter five.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Writing Object.create and instanceof by Hand
text: Now instanceof. The expression `obj instanceof Ctor` asks, does Ctor.prototype appear anywhere in obj's prototype chain? So our myInstanceOf takes obj and Ctor. If obj is not an object, return false. Take `const target = Ctor.prototype`, then `let current = Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`, and loop. If current is null, return false. If current is strictly equal to target, return true. Otherwise move up. That's it. The real operator also checks for a Symbol dot hasInstance method first, which lets a class customize the test, but the chain walk is the core.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Writing Object.create and instanceof by Hand
text: Here's a bonus that connects to something you'll see in real codebases. Object.create takes an optional second argument, a map of property descriptors, so you can define properties that are not writable or not enumerable at creation time. We won't implement descriptors, but it's worth knowing they exist, since Object.defineProperty is what class syntax uses under the hood for its non-enumerable methods. If you want an extra challenge, extend myCreate to accept a descriptor map and apply each entry with defineProperty.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Writing Object.create and instanceof by Hand
text: Let's test with the classes from the last lecture. A dog is an instance of Dog, of Animal and of Object, and not of Array. Now the sneaky case. Create dog, then reassign `Dog.prototype = {}`. Now `dog instanceof Dog` is false, because the chain no longer contains the new prototype object. This is a classic reason instanceof lies across realms too, like between iframes, where each frame has its own Array. That's why Array.isArray exists. You now own two core pieces of the language. Next chapter, we leave the language and look at the engine under it.

lecture_title: 5.1 - V8 Engine and Hidden Classes
text: We now step under the language, into V8, the engine that runs inside Chrome and Node. So far we've modeled how JavaScript behaves. In this chapter we ask how it can be fast, because the model we built, walking chains and looking up names in maps, sounds slow. And it would be, if the engine really did that every time. Let's see how it avoids it, starting with the single most important idea in the engine's object representation.

lecture_title: 5.1 - V8 Engine and Hidden Classes
text: V8, the JavaScript engine inside Node.js and Chrome, uses hidden classes to optimize property access on objects. When you create an object and add properties to it, V8 creates an internal hidden class that describes the shape of that object. Hidden classes are similar to structs in C. Every time you add a new property to an object V8 creates a new hidden class and transitions the object to it. This is how V8 avoids the overhead of a hash table lookup on every property access and can instead use fast fixed-offset memory access.

lecture_title: 5.1 - V8 Engine and Hidden Classes
text: Let me draw this out. Imagine `const p = {}`. V8 gives it an initial hidden class, call it C0, describing an empty shape. Then `p.x = 1` creates a new hidden class C1, which says there is a property x at offset zero, and records the transition from C0 to C1 on the key x. Then `p.y = 2` makes C2, with x at offset zero and y at offset one, via a transition from C1. The object itself now stores just the values in order, and a pointer to its current hidden class. The shape lives in one place, shared by everyone with that shape.

lecture_title: 5.1 - V8 Engine and Hidden Classes
text: The critical thing to understand about V8 hidden classes is that two objects that look identical to you can end up with completely different hidden classes if you add properties in a different order. If you create object A and add x then y, and create object B and add y then x, V8 sees them as different shapes and cannot optimize them the same way. This also means dynamically adding properties after object construction, especially in conditionals or loops, causes hidden class transitions that hurt performance significantly in hot code paths.

lecture_title: 5.1 - V8 Engine and Hidden Classes
text: You can actually see this. In Node, run a script with the flag `--allow-natives-syntax` and call `%HaveSameMap(a, b)`, which returns true if two objects share a hidden class. Create `a = { x: 1, y: 2 }` and `b = { x: 3, y: 4 }`, same literal, and it's true. Now create `c = { y: 4, x: 3 }` and the result is false against a. Same keys, same values, different order, different shape. It's the cleanest demonstration I know. And in our mini-runtime we'll add a small shapes.js that records transitions, so you can print the shape chain yourself.

lecture_title: 5.1 - V8 Engine and Hidden Classes
text: Let me do that now. In shapes.js, a class Shape with an id, a Map called transitions, and a Map called offsets. A function addProperty takes a shape and a key. If the shape already has a transition for the key, return it, otherwise create a new Shape that copies offsets and adds the key at the next offset, store it in transitions, and return it. Create a root shape, add x, add y, and again from the root add y, add x. Print ids, and you'll see two separate branches, which is exactly the situation the engine finds itself in.

lecture_title: 5.1 - V8 Engine and Hidden Classes
text: To write V8-friendly code, always initialize all object properties in the constructor in the same order every time. Never add new properties to an object after construction if you can avoid it. Avoid delete operator on properties as it forces V8 to switch to a slower dictionary mode. Prefer setting a property to null instead of deleting it. When you follow these patterns V8 can share hidden classes across all instances of the same constructor, leading to significant speedups through inline caching and JIT compilation.

lecture_title: 5.1 - V8 Engine and Hidden Classes
text: There's one practical thing I want to leave you with. Don't over-apply this. Hidden classes matter in hot code, meaning loops and functions called thousands of times, with many objects of the same kind, like particles or rows. In code that runs once, shape consistency changes nothing you can measure. Profile first. Next lecture, we find out what V8 does with these shapes at each property access, which is inline caching, and why code that sees only one shape is the fastest of all.

lecture_title: 5.2 - Inline Caches and Monomorphic Code
text: In the last lecture we learned that V8 gives every object a hidden class. But a shape by itself doesn't make anything fast. It's what V8 does with that shape at each property access site that matters. Today we study inline caches, and the terms monomorphic, polymorphic and megamorphic, which you'll see in performance articles and profiling tools. And then we'll simulate an inline cache in mini-runtime so you can watch it hit and miss.

lecture_title: 5.2 - Inline Caches and Monomorphic Code
text: Consider a function `function getX(p) { return p.x }`. The first time it runs, V8 doesn't know where x lives in p, so it does the slow generic lookup. But then it remembers. At that exact spot in the code, it stores a small cache, saying, if the object's hidden class is C1, then x is at offset zero. That's an inline cache. The next call checks one thing, is this object's hidden class C1, and if so, reads memory at offset zero directly. One comparison and one load, no lookup, no prototype walk.

lecture_title: 5.2 - Inline Caches and Monomorphic Code
text: Now the states. If the site has only ever seen one hidden class, it's monomorphic, the fastest state. If it has seen two to four different classes, it's polymorphic, and the cache holds a short list that it checks one by one, still decent. If it sees more than that, it becomes megamorphic and falls back to a shared global lookup table, and that is significantly slower. And the optimizing compiler, TurboFan, can inline and optimize the monomorphic sites best, because it can bake in the assumption about the shape.

lecture_title: 5.2 - Inline Caches and Monomorphic Code
text: Let's simulate this in mini-runtime. In shapes.js I'll add makeSite, which returns a function with a cache array. When called with an object, it reads the object's shape. If the shape is in the cache, it increments hits and returns the value from the stored offset. Otherwise it does the slow lookup, increments misses, pushes the shape into the cache, and if the cache grows beyond four entries, it sets a flag called megamorphic and stops caching. Feed it fifty objects of one shape and print the stats, forty-nine hits and one miss.

lecture_title: 5.2 - Inline Caches and Monomorphic Code
text: Let me give you some honest guidance on what to do with this. Don't contort your code to chase monomorphism everywhere. Do three simple things. Create objects of the same kind with the same constructor or factory, so they share a shape. Initialize all fields up front, even if the value is null for now. And avoid passing wildly different object kinds through a hot function, split it when it makes sense. Beyond that, measure with a profiler, because engine details change from version to version, and the principles last longer than the specifics.

lecture_title: 5.2 - Inline Caches and Monomorphic Code
text: Now feed it objects built with different key orders, five different shapes, and watch it go megamorphic and the miss counter climb. This is why a function that handles very different object kinds, like a general utility called with everything in your app, is slower than several specialized ones. It's also why TypeScript style discipline, consistent object shapes, helps performance as a side effect. We'll use this when we trace a bug through the layers at the end of the course. Right now though, we move to the other half of the story, the event loop.

lecture_title: 6.1 - The Event Loop and Microtasks
text: Welcome to chapter six, the one that explains why JavaScript can wait for a network request without freezing. So far everything we've modeled has been synchronous, one call after another, on one stack. But real programs have timers, clicks and fetches. To handle them, the runtime wraps the engine in a loop, and today we'll understand that loop precisely, including the part with promises that catches out even experienced people. Let's start with the definition, and then we'll test it.

lecture_title: 6.1 - The Event Loop and Microtasks
text: JavaScript runs on a single thread, so it can only do one thing at a time. The event loop is the mechanism that lets it stay responsive despite that. There is a call stack where function calls are pushed and popped, and a task queue (the macrotask queue) where callbacks from things like setTimeout, I/O, and DOM events wait. The event loop has one simple rule: when the call stack is empty, take the next task from the queue and run it to completion. 'Run to completion' is key — a task is never interrupted halfway, which is why long synchronous work freezes the page.

lecture_title: 6.1 - The Event Loop and Microtasks
text: Let's check it with a classic puzzle. Write console.log one, then setTimeout with a callback logging two and a delay of zero, then console.log three. The output is one, three, two. Why? The main script is itself a task. It runs to completion, logging one and three, and the timer callback sits in the macrotask queue until the stack is empty. Note that a delay of zero doesn't mean now, it means as soon as possible after the current task, and browsers and Node also enforce a small minimum.

lecture_title: 6.1 - The Event Loop and Microtasks
text: Promises do not use the macrotask queue. They use a separate, higher-priority microtask queue. After every single task finishes and before the event loop picks up the next macrotask, it completely drains the microtask queue. This is why a resolved Promise's .then callback always runs before a setTimeout(fn, 0) scheduled at the same time — microtasks jump the line. The practical consequence: if you schedule microtasks that themselves schedule more microtasks, you can starve the macrotask queue and block rendering. await is just syntax over .then, so the code after an await also runs as a microtask.

lecture_title: 6.1 - The Event Loop and Microtasks
text: Now the real puzzle. Script logs start, then setTimeout logging timeout, then `Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise'))`, then logs end. The output is start, end, promise, timeout. Walk through it. The script task logs start and end. Its callbacks are registered, the timer in the macrotask queue and the promise reaction in the microtask queue. When the script task finishes, the microtask queue is drained, so promise prints. Only then does the loop take the timer task. Practice drawing the two queues on paper for a few programs, until it's automatic.

lecture_title: 6.1 - The Event Loop and Microtasks
text: Let me show the starvation problem I mentioned. Write a function `function loop() { Promise.resolve().then(loop) }` and call it. The page, or in Node the whole process, never gets to timers or I/O, because the microtask queue never becomes empty. It's an infinite loop that doesn't look like one, since each step is asynchronous. Compare this with `setTimeout(loop, 0)`, which lets other tasks and rendering interleave. Node adds one more detail, process.nextTick has its own queue that runs even before promise microtasks. We'll keep that outside our model but know it exists.

lecture_title: 6.1 - The Event Loop and Microtasks
text: So, to summarize what we need to build. A call stack, which we have. A macrotask queue, a microtask queue, and a loop that runs one task, then drains microtasks, then repeats. In the browser there's also a rendering step between tasks, which is why long tasks cause janky pages. Next lecture we code all of that in eventloop.js, and then we'll run the puzzles from today through our own simulator and see the same output. If you want to prepare, think about what data structure each queue should be.

lecture_title: 6.2 - Writing an Event Loop Simulator
text: Today we write eventloop.js. In the last lecture we described the machine in words, two queues and a loop. Now we make it real, and by the end you'll run the setTimeout and promise puzzles through your own simulator and get exactly the output Node gives. I think this is the most satisfying lecture in the course, because it's short code that explains a huge amount of real-world behavior. So open your editor, create eventloop.js, and follow along with me.

lecture_title: 6.2 - Writing an Event Loop Simulator
text: Let's set up the pieces. In eventloop.js I'll create a class EventLoop with three fields. `macrotasks`, an array used as a queue, `microtasks`, another array, and `timers`, a list of objects with a callback and a due time, plus a `now` field that is our fake clock. Using a fake clock is a deliberate choice, because it makes the simulator deterministic, and we can test it without waiting. Then methods. `setTimeout(fn, delay)` pushes `{ fn, due: this.now + delay }` into timers, and `queueMicrotask(fn)` pushes fn into microtasks.

lecture_title: 6.2 - Writing an Event Loop Simulator
text: Now the heart, the method run. It takes the main script as a function. First, wrap the script as the first macrotask by pushing it to macrotasks. Then a loop. While there is any work, meaning macrotasks, timers or microtasks left, do the following. If the macrotask queue is empty, advance now to the earliest due timer and move every timer that is due into macrotasks, sorted by due time and insertion order. Then shift one macrotask and run it to completion. Then call drainMicrotasks, and repeat. That's one turn of the loop.

lecture_title: 6.2 - Writing an Event Loop Simulator
text: The drain is a small piece. `drainMicrotasks()` does `while (this.microtasks.length) { const fn = this.microtasks.shift(); fn(); }`. Notice that it keeps going even when fn pushes new microtasks, because the length is checked each time. That single detail reproduces the starvation behavior we discussed. I'll also add a guard counter in our simulator that throws after a million microtasks, so our own infinite-microtask test doesn't hang the terminal. A real engine has no such guard, which is exactly why it hangs.

lecture_title: 6.2 - Writing an Event Loop Simulator
text: Let's extend the simulator one step further, to see how a promise fits in. I'll write a tiny class MyPromise in eventloop.js with a state, a value and a list of callbacks. Its then method, if the promise is already settled, calls loop dot queueMicrotask with the callback, otherwise it stores the callback to be queued on resolve. Resolve sets the state and queues every stored callback as a microtask. That's the whole trick. Native promises are more careful about thenables and error handling, but the scheduling idea is exactly this.

lecture_title: 6.2 - Writing an Event Loop Simulator
text: Let's run the puzzle. Write a script function that logs start, calls loop dot setTimeout with a callback logging timeout and a delay of zero, calls loop dot queueMicrotask with one logging promise, and logs end. Pass it to loop dot run. Output, start, end, promise, timeout. Now add a second timer with a smaller delay and see it fire first, and a microtask scheduled inside a timer callback and see it run right after that callback, before the next timer. Same as the real thing. Next time we use this machine to understand async and await, which is simply a friendlier way to write promise chains.

lecture_title: 6.3 - async/await Is Just .then Underneath
text: In this lecture we finish chapter six by putting a friendly face on the machine. Async and await look like a different feature, almost like threads, but they're built from promises, and promises are built on the microtask queue we just simulated. The takeaway statement, and I want you to say it with me, is that await is just then underneath. We'll prove it by rewriting async functions as then chains and by predicting some tricky output order.

lecture_title: 6.3 - async/await Is Just .then Underneath
text: Start with the basics. An async function always returns a promise. If it returns a value, the promise resolves with it, and if it throws, the promise rejects. Inside, the await keyword pauses that function, not the thread. It takes a promise, or wraps a plain value in a resolved promise, and arranges for the rest of the function to run as a microtask continuation when the promise settles. Meanwhile the caller carries on. That's why code after calling an async function runs before the code after the await inside it.

lecture_title: 6.3 - async/await Is Just .then Underneath
text: Here's a puzzle. `async function f() { console.log('a'); await null; console.log('b'); }`, then call f, then log c. The output is a, c, b. Step by step. Calling f runs synchronously up to the first await, so a prints. The await schedules the continuation as a microtask and returns control to the caller, which prints c. Then the stack is empty, the microtask runs, and b prints. The equivalent without async is `console.log('a'); Promise.resolve(null).then(() => console.log('b'))`. Same order, same mechanism.

lecture_title: 6.3 - async/await Is Just .then Underneath
text: Let's make it more interesting by mixing with a timer. Add a setTimeout logging t before the call to f. Now the output is a, c, b, t. The microtask continuation, b, always beats the timer. And if f awaits a promise that resolves from a timer, say a promise that resolves inside setTimeout with a delay of fifty, then the continuation waits for that timer task, and after the timer callback finishes its microtasks drain, and b prints. In our simulator you can verify all this by writing the promise logic ourselves as a tiny class with then, using queueMicrotask, in about twenty lines.

lecture_title: 6.3 - async/await Is Just .then Underneath
text: Let me summarize with a translation rule you can use whenever you are confused. Take an async function, and split its body at each await. Everything before the first await runs synchronously when called. Each remaining piece becomes a function passed to then on the awaited promise, and the function's returned promise resolves with whatever the last piece returns. A try and catch around an await becomes a catch on the chain. If you can do that translation in your head, you can predict any ordering question an interviewer or a bug throws at you.

lecture_title: 6.3 - async/await Is Just .then Underneath
text: Two practical warnings. First, await inside a loop makes iterations sequential. If the operations are independent, collect the promises and use Promise.all, so they run concurrently. Second, an error thrown after an await is a rejected promise, so wrap the awaited code in try and catch, or the rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection, which crashes modern Node by default. Also, forgetting to await a promise is silent, the code after just keeps going. Now we have all the layers, stack, scope, prototypes, shapes and loop. In the final chapter, we'll use them together.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Tracing One Bug Through Every Layer
text: This is the capstone. For six chapters we built pieces of mini-runtime, and in this lecture I want you to see them work together on a realistic bug. I'll show you a small program that misbehaves in a confusing way, and we'll debug it by asking at each layer what the model says should happen. The point isn't the bug itself, it's the method, going down through the layers until the surprise disappears. So let's get started.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Tracing One Bug Through Every Layer
text: Here's the program. A small task tracker, with a class Task, created with a title and a list of tags. A function loadTasks that runs a loop for each id, and calls fetchTask with a delay, using setTimeout in the callback to push results into an array called results. After the loop, the code logs results dot length and expects three, but prints zero. Also, a second symptom, when tasks finally appear, every one has the same id. Two bugs, one program, and they sit in different layers.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Tracing One Bug Through Every Layer
text: Take the first symptom, results dot length is zero. Which layer? The event loop. The callbacks passed to setTimeout are macrotasks, they run only after the current script task finishes and the stack is empty. The log line runs in the current task, so results is still empty. It's not a timing mystery, it's the run-to-completion rule. We confirm by running the program through our EventLoop simulator, and the log happens before any timer callback. The fix is to return a promise, await all the work, and only then log.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Tracing One Bug Through Every Layer
text: Second symptom, every task has the same id. Which layer? Scope and closures. The loop uses var i, and the setTimeout callback closes over i. By the time any callback runs, the loop has finished and i is three, and all callbacks share the single function-level scope. In our Scope model, there's one binding for i. Switch to let, each iteration gets its own block scope with its own i, and each closure captures its own. We can demonstrate this in runtime.js by creating a new Scope per iteration.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Tracing One Bug Through Every Layer
text: Let me put the fixed version together so you can compare. The Task constructor now sets title, id and tags in one fixed order, with tags defaulting to an empty array. The loadTasks function is async, uses a for of loop with let, and awaits Promise.all over the fetches, then logs the length, three. Run it and the numbers are right, the ids are distinct, and a profile shows a single shape for Task. The skill here wasn't memorizing fixes, it was asking, which layer is responsible, and answering from the model.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Tracing One Bug Through Every Layer
text: Now a third, quieter issue that shows up in profiling. Tasks created in loadTasks sometimes have a tags property and sometimes not, depending on the data, and the code adds tags afterward when present. Which layer? Hidden classes. Objects of the same class end up with two shapes, so a hot function reading task dot tags sees two shapes, polymorphic, and if more variations appear, megamorphic. The fix is to always initialize tags in the constructor, to an empty array if there are none. Three symptoms, three layers, and no magic involved.

lecture_title: 7.2 - Where from Here?
text: Well, we made it to the end. Let me start by saying congratulations, because you did something most JavaScript developers never do. You looked under the hood, and not just looked, you rebuilt it. Let me recap what mini-runtime contains now. A callstack.js with frames and stack traces. A scope.js with the scope chain, hoisting and closures. A proto.js with prototype lookup, classes, and hand-written create and instanceof. A shapes.js with hidden class transitions and inline caches. And an eventloop.js with macrotasks, microtasks and a fake clock.

lecture_title: 7.2 - Where from Here?
text: Let me also summarize the mental models, because those are the real product. Execution is a stack of contexts. Names are resolved by walking a chain of scopes determined by where code is written. The value of this is determined by how a function is called, except for arrows. Objects delegate to their prototypes at runtime, and classes are sugar over that. The engine assigns shapes, and rewards consistency. And everything asynchronous goes through two queues, with microtasks always drained between tasks. If you can explain each of those without notes, you've learned the course.

lecture_title: 7.2 - Where from Here?
text: Here's what I'd suggest you do next. First, extend mini-runtime on your own. Add getters and setters to proto.js, so lookups invoke accessor functions. Add generators or async iteration to the event loop. Add a simple garbage collector that marks scopes reachable from the stack and sweeps the rest, which makes closures and memory leaks very concrete. Each of these is a weekend project, and each teaches you something that reading never will. Don't try to make it complete, it's a teaching model, and the gaps are where you learn.

lecture_title: 7.2 - Where from Here?
text: Second, go and read primary sources. The ECMAScript specification is more readable than people think, especially the sections on function calls and the abstract operations like OrdinaryGet, which is literally our prototype lookup. The V8 blog has excellent posts on hidden classes, Ignition and TurboFan, and the Node.js docs on the event loop describe the phases in detail. When you read them now, you'll recognize every concept, and the vocabulary won't be a barrier anymore. Use Chrome devtools and node dash dash inspect to look at real scope chains and profiles as well.

lecture_title: 7.2 - Where from Here?
text: Let me end with one honest note on learning. You will forget details, and that's fine. What stays is the shape of the model, and your ability to rebuild a piece of it when you need it. When you meet a new framework, ask what it does with scope, with this, with objects, and with the event loop, because every framework is a set of choices about those same five things. Thank you again, and keep building. Share your mini-runtime extensions with other learners, teaching it back is the best way to lock it in.

lecture_title: 7.2 - Where from Here?
text: Third, use this in your daily work. The next time you see a confusing bug, ask which layer it lives in. Stack, scope, this, prototype, shape or queue. That habit alone will make you faster at debugging than most of your peers. And if you want to go deeper, we have courses on browser APIs and on React performance, which apply exactly these ideas. Thank you for building this with me. Go and break something in mini-runtime on purpose and fix it. I'll see you in the next course.
